food.text: In December 2020, Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia won UNESCO recognition for the knowledge, know-how and practices of making and eating couscous. It was placed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The joint submission was hailed as an "example of international cooperation."

Couscous entered French and European cuisine at the beginning of the twentieth century. It travelled through the French colonial empire and the Pieds-Noirs of Algeria. The earliest French mention of the word dates to the 16th century, but the dish itself only became part of French cooking in the 20th.

Maghrebi mint tea is central to social life in the Maghreb. It is made from gunpowder green tea, spearmint and sugar, and is traditionally prepared by the head male of the family and offered to guests as a sign of hospitality. Typically at least three glasses are served.
Couscous is widely eaten in France, where Maghreb immigrants introduced it. In a 2011 survey it was voted the third most popular dish in the country.

Harissa, a paste of ground chili peppers, garlic and caraway or other spices, is used extensively in Tunisian cooking and is often the most important ingredient in sauces and gravies. It has been on UNESCO's list of Intangible Heritage since 2022.
The tajine is a clay cooking vessel found across the Maghreb, but the dishes made in it vary widely. In Tunisia a tajine is a baked, quiche-like dish, whereas in Morocco it is a slow-cooked stew.
Amlu is a Moroccan spread of toasted, crushed almonds kneaded with honey and argan oil. It is usually served at breakfast or afternoon tea with pancakes and pastries.

In Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, couscous is generally served with vegetables such as carrots, potatoes and turnips cooked in a spicy or mild broth. Meat, usually chicken, lamb or mutton, often goes with it. A larger variety over 3 mm across is known as berkoukes.

European settlers introduced potatoes to Tunisia in the early 20th century. They became a common ingredient in traditional salads, sauces and couscous. By 1990 one of the most common homemade potato foods was French fries.

Couscous sold in most Western grocery stores is pre-steamed and dried. It is prepared by adding 1.5 measures of boiling water or stock per measure of couscous and covering it tightly for about five minutes. European supermarkets also routinely sell packaged quick-preparation sets with canned vegetables.

People in Sfax, Tunisia, still favor traditional dishes despite the strong presence of fast food. A local staple is marka, a fish soup to which vermicelli or couscous is usually added. Charmoula, made of baked raisins, onions and spices, is traditionally eaten with salted fish on the first day of Eid al-Fitr.

Sfax is famed for its pastries, which come in two kinds. Everyday sweets are called hlou Arbi and include makrouth, doria and ghraiba. Finer pastries such as baklawa, mlabbes and ka'ak warka' are made for weddings and special ceremonies.

art.text: Morocco's modern architecture includes early 20th-century Art Deco and neo-Moorish buildings constructed during the French and Spanish colonial occupation between 1912 and 1956. After independence, some new buildings still paid tribute to traditional Moroccan architecture and motifs, even when foreign architects designed them.

France invaded Tunisia in 1881 and imposed the French Protectorate, which lasted until 1956. In Tunis the French built a new planned city outside the existing walled city rather than demolishing the old one. The old city became known as the medina and the new one as the Ville Nouvelle. In Algiers, by contrast, the French demolished much of the old city after 1830 to build their own colonial edifices.

Berber jewellery was usually made of silver and included elaborate triangular plates and pins, originally used as clasps for garments. Women handed it down from generation to generation as a visual element of Berber ethnic identity. During the second part of the 20th century, the tradition was gradually abandoned.

The Bardo National Museum in Tunis holds one of the largest collections of Roman mosaics in the world. Many came from excavations begun in the early 20th century at sites including Carthage, Hadrumetum, Dougga and Utica. The mosaics are a unique source for research on everyday life in Roman Africa.

The Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, completed in 1993, is a massive building that pays tribute to traditional Moroccan architecture and motifs. The Mausoleum of King Mohammed V, completed in 1971, does the same, even though foreign architects sometimes designed such buildings.

French colonial architects in Tunisia often built in what they considered the Arab style, called arabisant. It ranged from extravagant pastiches of Moorish architecture to more academic designs based on study of the country's indigenous architecture. It appeared on railway stations, post offices, law courts and some private villas.

The Institut du Monde arabe in Paris exhibited more than 250 pieces of mainly Berber jewelry from Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia from February 2016 to January 2017. The private-collection show was titled Des trésors à porter. Bijoux et parures du Maghreb.
One lavish example of arabisant architecture is a villa designed by the Italian millionaire Georges Sebastian in 1939 to 1940. It stands near Hammamet in Tunisia.

The Bardo museum underwent a major refurbishment completed in 2012, interrupted by the Tunisian revolution. The expansion added 9,000 square meters and was designed by SCPA Codou-Hindley of France and Amira Nouira of Tunisia. Considerable funding came from the World Bank.

The French ethnologist Henriette Camps-Fabrer wrote several books about the Berber jewellery of Algeria and neighbouring countries between the 1970s and 1990. After Algerian independence in 1962, she and her husband Gabriel Camps taught at the University of Algiers. Gabriel Camps founded the Encyclopédie Berbère, which published her entries on Berber jewellery.

war.text: An Islamist insurgency began in the Maghreb after the Algerian Civil War ended in 2002. The Algerian group GSPC allied itself with al-Qaeda and eventually became al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM). The insurgency brought mass killing: the GSPC ambushed convoys and killed soldiers and civilians, and AQIM later used suicide bombers, such as the two suicide truck bombers who killed 37 people at U.N. offices in Algiers in December 2007. Since 2007, when Operation Enduring Freedom – Trans Sahara began, Maghreb governments have worked with the United States and the United Kingdom against the militants.

Since 2015, Tunisia has been targeted by an Islamic State insurgency campaign, while also fighting other militants. In March 2016, over 50 militants were killed when IS fighters tried to seize Ben Guerdane, near the Libya–Tunisia border. The article's timeline for that month also records a soldier and four citizens killed when IS jihadists attacked a border town on the Libya–Tunisia border.

Fighting in Algeria stayed deadly after 2002. Over 1,100 people were killed in clashes with Islamist rebels in 2002, then 1,162 in 2003, 429 in 2004, 488 in 2005 and 323 in 2006. In early 2006 the head of the national police claimed terrorism had nearly been eliminated, but significant attacks continued, and 2007 marked a height of suicide bombings and terrorist attacks in Algeria.

In 2014, militants of the Uqba ibn Nafi Brigade attacked two Tunisian military checkpoints. They killed fourteen Tunisian soldiers and injured twenty-five, in what was the deadliest military skirmish in Tunisia since its independence in 1956.

The British attack on the French fleet at Mers-el-Kebir on 3 July 1940 removed a potential threat, but it discouraged other French units from joining the Free French. French West Africa, along with the North African colonies, Syria and Indochina, remained under Vichy control.

On 18 March 2015, three gunmen in civil uniform attacked the Bardo National Museum and took hostages. Twenty-one people, mostly European tourists, were killed at the scene, and one more victim died ten days later, making 24 dead, with around fifty others injured. Two of the gunmen, Tunisian citizens Yassine Labidi and Saber Khachnaoui, were killed by police, while the third escaped. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Tunisian history, surpassing the 2002 Ghriba synagogue bombing, which killed nineteen people.

Mauritania lacked military resources, partly because of turmoil and because it has little population in a very large country. To defeat AQIM it relied on support from France, Morocco and Algeria. Attacks there have been largely thwarted since 2011, though AQIM stayed active in the eastern border regions with Mali.

Since 2012, the Tunisian Army has targeted AQIM, Ansar al-Sharia and the Uqba ibn Nafi Brigade in the Chaambi Operations. These militants were active in the mountainous Jebel ech Chambi region outside Kasserine, near the Algeria–Tunisia border.

The Islamic State managed to control some limited territory in Libya during the Second Libyan Civil War. There were allegations that it collaborated locally with its rival AQIM, even though the two groups were competitors.

literature.text: In 2005 the Algerian novelist Assia Djebar was elected to the Académie Française, the first writer from the Maghreb to receive that recognition. She had also won the 1996 Neustadt International Prize for Literature for her whole body of work.

Marie-Louise Belarbi, born in France, spent most of her life in Morocco, where in 1984 she founded the Casablanca bookstore Carrefour des Livres. With actor Bichr Bennani she also created the Tarik Publishing House to publish writing from Morocco and the Maghreb.

Abdelkebir Khatibi's Plural Maghreb, first published in 1983, is a book of six critical essays on language, translation, orientalism, power and decolonization. He presents the Maghreb as a horizon of thought and a model for plurality, and calls for a radicalization of the margin.
Assia Djebar was born Fatima-Zohra Imalayen in Cherchell, Algeria. In 1957 she chose her pen name for her first novel, La Soif (The Thirst), and a second book, Les Impatients, followed the next year.

Tarik Publishing House published early works by writers such as Tahar Ben Jelloun, Driss Chraïbi and Abdellah Taïa. It was also notable for publishing several prison memoirs, including Ahmed Marzouki's On affame bien les rats.

In 1994 Marie-Louise Belarbi was one of the founders of the Maghreb Book Fair, held in Paris every year and hosting over a hundred authors. From 1986 to 1990 she also hosted a literature television program called Plaisir de Lire.

Khatibi's essay Pensée-autre first appeared as Le Maghreb comme horizon de pensée in a 1977 special issue of Les Temps modernes produced by North African intellectuals. It develops the concept of Other Thought, which subverts both Western colonial legacy and Arab-Islamic heritage.

Assia Djebar attended the École normale supérieure de jeunes filles in 1955, becoming the first Algerian and Muslim woman educated at one of France's most elite schools. Her studies were interrupted by the Algerian War, and she later continued her education in Tunis.
tags: École normale supérieure de jeunes filles

literature.text: In her 1985 book L'Amour, la fantasia, Assia Djebar repeatedly states her ambivalence about language and about her identity as a Western-educated, Algerian, feminist, Muslim intellectual. It was translated into English as Fantasia: An Algerian Cavalcade by Dorothy S. Blair and published by Heinemann in 1993.

Before moving to Morocco, Marie-Louise Belarbi worked at the Paris publisher Éditions Julliard. There she accepted Françoise Sagan's first book, Bonjour tristesse, and convinced René Julliard to read and publish it.

In L'orientalisme désorienté, originally published in 1974, Khatibi criticizes the French sociologist Jacques Berque. Unlike Edward Said, who attacked those hostile toward the East, Khatibi targets Orientalists who romanticize it, which he sees as advancing the interests of Western technocracy.

Khatibi's Double critique essay engages with the thinking of Ibn Khaldun, arguing that it had been misappropriated by both Western and Islamic schools of social theory. An English translation of Plural Maghreb by P. Burcu Yalim was published by Bloomsbury in 2019.

science.text: The Maghreb Virtual Science Library gave researchers in the Maghreb full-text access to thousands of science and engineering journals and databases through digital library portals. The project was funded by the U.S. Department of State and implemented by CRDF Global.

Mauritanian researchers established a Center for Research in Renewable Energy at the University of Nouakchott and received an international award for malaria research. Science and engineering students in Mauritania account for more than 1/3 of university degree program enrollments.
tags: Center for Research in Renewable Energy

science.text: In Libya, scientists have transformed the research base to focus on national and regional challenges in areas such as water resources, renewable energy, and medicine. The Maghreb Virtual Science Library program planned to include Libya as circumstances and funding permit.

MVSL Open is a free gateway for everyone in the Maghreb to reach research publications and databases usually available only within universities. Its topics range from law and music to patent searching and the latest scientific discoveries.

In 2022, the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report listed the Medina of Sousse in Tunisia among African cultural sites that could be threatened by flooding and coastal erosion by the end of the century. This applied only under the RCP 8.5 scenario, which is no longer considered very likely.

Starting from 17 June 2014, the Bardo National Museum in Tunis offered visitors a digital guide in English, French, and Arabic. Developed by Orange Tunisia using Near-field communication technology, it was a free smartphone application with audio commentaries and photo slideshows.

The Maghreb Virtual Science Library began by working with Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. Its partners included IMIST, LibHub, Research4Life, and JSTOR, and it ran consultations and workshops so users could get the most from the system.
Charles Saumagne drew the plan of the Roman city of Carthage as early as 1924, thanks to his observations of the terrain. The plan remains largely valid even after the latest excavation campaigns.

Even if global warming is limited to 1.5 °C, sea level rise is still expected to exceed 2–3 m after 2000 years. Unless adaptation efforts such as sea walls are built, damage and potential destruction of the Medina of Sousse is described as a matter of time.

politics.text: Under French colonial rule, Morocco's Alawi sultans continued to act as nominal monarchs. Morocco regained independence in 1956 with Sultan Mohammed V as its sovereign. In 1957 he formally adopted the title of "King", and the country is now officially the Kingdom of Morocco.

As Pan-Arabism grew in the early 20th century, the political influence of European colonial powers in the Maghreb began to sharply decline. As Arab unity increased, so did opposition to any form of colonialism. Many Arab leaders saw Zionism as a continuation of European colonialism, because most early Zionist migrants came from Europe.

In February 1985, Ugo Vetere, the mayor of Rome, and Chedly Klibi, the mayor of Carthage, signed a symbolic treaty. It "officially" ended the conflict between their cities, which had supposedly lasted more than 2,100 years for lack of a peace treaty.

Political Islam was introduced in Mauritania in the 1970s. Instability after the coup that deposed Moktar Ould Daddah in 1978 invited elements of the Muslim Brotherhood, Wahabbism and Tablighi Jamaat. Islamists united as a political party in the 1980s but were politically repressed from 1994, and government pressure on Islamist organizations continued throughout the 2000s. In 2005, Islamists were arrested and accused of terrorism; of the original eighty arrested, eighteen were still in prison by 2006.

Decolonization in Tunisia, the independence war in Algeria and the rise of the Moroccan Army of Liberation all took place in the 1950s. Facing these pressures, the French agreed to negotiate Morocco's independence at a conference on August 23, 1955.

Shortly after Tunisian independence in 1956, a government decree aimed to eliminate all confessional tribunals, including courts based on Sharia law. It also abolished the rabbinical tribunal and the Jewish community councils, which the Jewish community understood as a curtailment of their autonomy.
Tunisia's Jewish population stood at around 105,000 in 1948. It fell to around 20,000 by 1967, and a further 7,000 Jews immigrated to France. As of 2021, only around 1,000 Jews remain in Tunisia.

Colonel Mohamed Khouna Ould Haidalla, one of the participants in the military coup that ousted Moktar Ould Daddah in 1978, became head of Mauritania's government in 1980 and implemented Sharia law. His successor, Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya, reversed some of these changes, but was himself ousted in a military coup in 2005.

The exiled sultan Mohammed V landed at Rabat-Salé Airport at 11:42 am on November 16, 1955. The French-Moroccan Declaration of Independence was formally signed on March 2, 1956, and Tangier was reintegrated into Morocco later that year.

Habib Bourguiba worked to reassure Tunisia's Jews of their equal position, even including a Jewish nationalist, Albert Bessis, in his first cabinet. Yet he failed to curb anti-Jewish violence. After the Six-Day War in 1967, the Grand Synagogue of Tunis was looted and burned to the ground.

Morocco was officially called the Sharifian Sultanate, rendered in French as l'Empire chérifien according to the Treaty of Fes. That name stayed in official use until 1956, when Morocco regained its independence from colonial rule.

philosophy.text: In his 1983 book Plural Maghreb, Abdelkebir Khatibi imagined the Maghreb "as a horizon of thought" and a model for plurality, alterity and difference. He called for a "radicalization of the margin." The six essays address language, translation, orientalism, power and decolonization.

André Servier, a historian in French Algeria in the early 20th century, edited the newspaper La Dépêche de Constantine. He defended Modernity and European colonization. He championed Western philosophy as founded on freedom and enlightened reason.

Khatibi presented a "plural Maghreb" as both a historical reality and a desire restrained by two forces. These were the dominance of theological-nationalist authorities and of Orientalist colonial forces. His thinking is grounded in culture theory and philosophy of language.

Khatibi developed the concept of Other Thought, or pensée autre. It is predicated on subverting the domination of both the Western colonial legacy and Arab-Islamic heritage. A version of the opening essay appeared in a 1977 special issue of Les Temps modernes produced by North African intellectuals.

Khatibi's thinking in Plural Maghreb was influenced by Jacques Derrida and his ideas on deconstruction and alterity. This linked a North African thinker's critique of colonial and religious authority to French philosophy.

Khatibi's essay Double critique engages with Ibn Khaldun. It argues that his thinking had been misappropriated by both Western and Islamic schools of social theory. The essay also studies colonial sociology and precolonial hierarchy in Morocco.

André Servier favored reflective morality against customary morality or authority-enforced puritanism. He held strong opinions about Islam and about the intellectual superiority of European thought. He saw himself as continuing Louis Bertrand's work, adapted to the Islamic background.

In L'orientalisme désorienté, originally published in 1974, Khatibi criticized Jacques Berque, a French sociologist and Arabist at the Collège de France. Unlike Edward Said, who attacked hostile Orientalists, Khatibi targeted those who romanticize the East. He saw this as advancing "the pecuniary interests of Western technocracy."

culture.text: The Maghreb once most commonly meant Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, the land between the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlas Mountains, and often also included eastern Libya. Only in recent decades was the definition expanded to include Mauritania and the disputed territory of Western Sahara.

Maghrebi Jews have lived in the northern Maghreb for more than 2,000 years, and their communities declined sharply in the mid-to-late 20th century. Morocco had the largest Jewish population in the Arab world, about 250,000 to 300,000 around the time Israel was established. Tunisia's Jewish population stood at around 105,000 in 1948 and about 1,000 as of 2021.

Algeria's Jewish community numbered about 140,000 before the Algerian War, but at independence in 1962 nearly all of them left the country. The 1870 Crémieux Decrees had given Jews full French citizenship, so most emigrated to France. In early 1977 a group of youths sacked the only remaining synagogue in Algiers.

Historian Christopher Silver wrote Recording History: Jews, Muslims, and Music across Twentieth-Century North Africa, published in 2022. Its publishers call it the first history of the music scene and recording industry across Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. Silver treats sound recordings as primary historical evidence rather than only as musical artifacts.

Algeria is overwhelmingly Sunni Muslim of the Maliki school, but surveys show a shift among the young. Arab Barometer found Algerians calling themselves non-religious rose from around 8% in 2013 to around 15% in 2018. A December 2019 follow-up found the growth was driven by young Algerians, with roughly 25% of that cohort describing themselves as non-religious.

Mauritania declared independence in 1960 and became an Islamic Republic, with Moktar Ould Daddah promoting Islam during his rule. A military coup d'état ousted Daddah in 1978, and Colonel Mohamed Khouna Ould Haidalla, one of its participants, became head of government in 1980 and implemented Sharia law. President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya, his successor, reversed some of these changes but was ousted in a military coup in 2005.

Shortly after Tunisian independence in 1956, a decree abolishing confessional tribunals also abolished rabbinical tribunals and Jewish community councils. Habib Bourguiba reassured Jews of their equal place in society and even put a Jewish nationalist, Albert Bessis, in his first cabinet. After the Six-Day War in 1967, however, the Grand Synagogue of Tunis was looted and burned to the ground.

Christopher Silver runs a website called Gharamophone, built on his personal archive of about 500 records by North African Jewish singers and instrumentalists. It lists artists, record companies, song titles and images of original record labels from the 1930s to 1950s. It also offers the free digital album Glimpses of North Africa's Musical Past: 1930-1956.
tags: Glimpses of North Africa's Musical Past

culture.text: The Baháʼí Faith in Algeria dates from 1952 and grew somewhat through 1967. At independence the country adopted Islamic practices in rejection of colonial influences, and the religion was effectively banned in 1968. Even so, by 2010 an estimated 3,300 Baháʼís lived in Algeria.
